title: "B" nurse
description: IV access and the "B" medicines: Captopril, Nitroglycerin, Salbutamol, glucose, Naloxone.

questions.q: Why do you need IV access?
answers: IV medicines (e.g. Glucose 40%) can only be given through a vein
Every patient needs it, so that the blood pressure can be measured
So that blood can be taken to measure the blood glucose on scene
Every medicine works faster through it, so all of them go there

questions.q: Which of the "B" medicines needs an IV?
answers: Glucose 40%
Captopril
Naloxone nasal spray
Nitroglycerin spray

questions.q: The cannulation failed. Can you reuse the same cannula?
answers: No, every attempt needs a new, sterile cannula
Yes, on the same patient, if the tip is not bent
Yes, once more, if it did not touch anything else
Yes, if you wipe it with alcohol before the next try

questions.q: Where do you first place a peripheral cannula in an adult?
answers: A vein on the back of the hand, the forearm or the elbow
A vein in the neck, because it is large and easy to see
A vein on the foot or the ankle, away from the injuries
The groin vein, because it is the largest and most sure
Lowering high blood pressure, under the tongue
Lowering high blood pressure, through the IV
Relieving chest pain by widening the vessels
Lowering a fast pulse, swallowed with water

questions.q: A suspected stroke patient's blood pressure is 190/100. Do you give Captopril?
answers: No: in a stroke we do not lower it between 130–220
Yes: it must go below 140 to prevent a brain bleed
Yes, half a dose, so that it only falls a little
No, but Nitroglycerin spray is given to lower it
Raising low blood glucose fast, through the IV
Raising low blood glucose slowly, by mouth
Replacing fluid in shock, as an IV infusion
Raising low blood glucose, into the muscle

questions.q: When can you give glucose gel?
answers: Only to an awake patient who can swallow
To an unconscious patient, into the cheek
To any hypoglycaemic patient, awake or not
When there is no IV, even if they are drowsy

questions.q: Unconscious patient, blood glucose 35 mg/dL. What do you give?
answers: Place an IV and give Glucose 40%
Glucose gel into the cheek pouch
Sweet drink in small sips, carefully
Nothing until the patient wakes up
Reversing an opioid (heroin, fentanyl) overdose
Reversing a sleeping pill (benzodiazepine) overdose
Reversing a stimulant (cocaine, amphetamine) overdose
Reversing alcohol poisoning with slow breathing

questions.q: Besides slow, shallow breathing, which sign shown in the picture points to an opioid overdose?
answers: Pinpoint pupils
Dilated pupils
Unequal pupils
Pupils not reacting to light

questions.q: What do you watch after giving Naloxone?
answers: It can wear off and the patient can fall asleep again: watch the breathing
The effect lasts for days, so once awake the patient can safely stay home
It raises the blood glucose strongly: measure it again every few minutes
It lowers the blood pressure a lot: lay the patient down and raise the legs
With low blood pressure (systolic below 90 mmHg)
With high blood pressure (systolic above 160 mmHg)
In pulmonary oedema with crackles and frothy sputum
With chest pain that started less than an hour ago

questions.q: In which condition does Nitroglycerin help?
answers: Pulmonary oedema (crackles, pink frothy sputum)
Asthma attack (wheezing, long breathing out)
Shock after bleeding (pale, cold, fast pulse)
Stroke with very high blood pressure (190/100)
Wheezing: asthma, COPD, nebulised
Crackles: pulmonary oedema, nebulised
Croup or airway swelling, as an injection
Allergic swelling of the throat, into the IV

questions.q: What do you check after placing a cannula?
answers: That fluid runs freely and the site does not swell
That blood flows back into the cannula, nothing else
That the patient feels no pain at the puncture site
That the pulse below the cannula can still be felt

questions.q: Swelling and pain appear around the cannula and the fluid does not run. What happened?
answers: The cannula slipped out of the vein: remove it and try at a new site
The cannula is blocked by a clot: flush it hard with a full syringe
The fluid runs too slowly: raise the bag higher and open the clamp
An allergy to the fluid: stop it and give the next medicine instead

questions.q: What do you check before giving any medicine?
answers: Right medicine, right dose, right route, right patient, and no allergy to it
Right medicine, right dose and the expiry date, the rest is checked later
The patient's name, weight and blood group, and that the IV is working
Right medicine and right route; the dose is the same for every patient
